text: Uniform and non-uniform circular motion. Uniform circular motion describes an object that travels in a circle with a constant speed. For example, any point on a propeller spinning at a constant rate is undergoing uniform circular motion, or a point on the edge of a spinning disc. Points on these rotating objects are actually accelerating, that is, changing direction, although the rotation rate is a constant. Centripetal acceleration. In one D kinematics, objects with a constant speed have zero acceleration. However, in 2D and 3D kinematics, a particle can have acceleration if it moves along a curved trajectory, for example, a circle with a constant speed. In this case, the velocity vector, vector V, is changing, or D vector V, DT, is not equal to zero. As a particle moves counterclockwise in time through an interval change in T on a circular path, bullet point, its position vector, vector R of T, moves from vector R of T to vector R of T plus change in T. Bullet point, its velocity vector, vector V, has a constant magnitude, V, and is tangent to the path as it changes from vector V of T to vector V of T plus change in T, only changing its direction, since the velocity vector, vector V of T, is perpendicular to the position vector, vector R of T. The triangles formed by the position vectors, along with its difference vector, change in R, and the velocity vector, vector V, along with its difference vector, change in V, are similar. Furthermore, the two triangles are isosceles. From these facts, we have change in R equals R change in theta, change in V equals V change in theta, change in V over V equals change in R over R. We can find the magnitude of the acceleration from change in V equals V change in R over R. The limit of sub change in T goes to 0, change in V over change in T, equals V over R, the limit of sub change in T goes to 0, change in R over change in T. Equals V over R, V equals V squared over R. A particle moving in a circle at a constant speed has an acceleration with magnitude A sub C equals V squared over R. Checkpoint. In uniform circular motion, the speed is constant. Why is the object still accelerating? The direction of the acceleration vector is pointed inwards toward the center of the circle. This is a radial acceleration because it's along the radial direction and is also called the centripetal acceleration. Note, the word centripetal comes from the Latin words centrum meaning center and pedare to mean to seek, and thus takes the meaning center seeking. Con Academy. Centripetal acceleration can have a wide range of values depending on the speed and radius of the circular path. Typical centripetal acceleration values are given in the following table. Table. A jet is flying at a speed of 134.1 meters per second along a straight line and then makes a turn along a circular path that is level with the ground. What does the radius of the circular path have to be to produce a centripetal acceleration of 1G on the pilot and jet toward the center of the circular trajectory? Expand the drop down below to see the worked solution. The model. The jet is modeled as moving at constant speed along a horizontal circular path. Since the speed is constant, the acceleration is centripetal and points toward the center of the circle. The required radius is found from the relationship between speed, turning radius, and centripetal acceleration. The math. For uniform circular motion, the centripetal acceleration depends on the square of the speed divided by the radius as a sub c equals v squared over r. The required acceleration is one gravitational acceleration. So the centripetal acceleration condition is g equals v squared over r. Multiplying both sides by r and then dividing both sides by g gives the required radius r equals v squared over g. Substituting the jet speed and g equals 9.81 meters per second squared gives the required turn radius r equals 134.1 meters per second squared over 9.81 meters per second squared equals 1830 meters or 1.83 kilometers. The conclusion. To produce a centripetal acceleration of 1g at a speed of 134.1 meters per second, the jet must follow a circular path with radius 1830 meters or 1.83 kilometers. The large radius shows why high speed turns require substantial horizontal space even when the acceleration is only comparable to ordinary gravity. The problem. A proton has speed 5.0 times 10 to the sixth meters per second and is moving in a circle in the xy plane of radius r equals 0.175 meters. What is its position in the xy plane at time t equals 2.0 times 10 to the minus 7 seconds equals 200 nanoseconds? At t equals 0, the position of the proton is 0.175 i hat meters and its circles counterclockwise. Sketch the trajectory. Expand the drop down below to see the worked solution. The model. The proton undergoes uniform circular motion in the xy plane. Its speed and radius are constant, so its angular position increases at a constant rate. Because the proton starts on the positive x axis and moves counterclockwise, the x component is represented by a cosine function and the y component is represented by a sine function. The math. For uniform circular motion, the angular frequency is the speed divided by the radius. Omega equals v over r. Substituting the given speed and radius gives the angular frequency omega equals 5.0 times 10 to the sixth meters per second over 0.175 meters equals 2.9 times 10 to the 7 rad per second. For counterclockwise motion, that begins at vector r of 0 equals r i hat. The position vector is written using cosine and sine components as vector r of t equals r cosine omega t i hat plus r sine omega t j hat. Multiplying the angular frequency by the elapsed time gives the angular position at t equals 2.0 times 10 to the minus 7 seconds. Omega t equals 2.9 times 10 to the 7 rad per second times 2.0 times 10 to the minus 7 seconds equals 5.7 rad. Substituting the angular position into the circular motion position vector gives the protons position vector r equals 0.175 meters cosine of 5.7 i hat plus 0.175 meters sine of 5.7 j hat equals 0.15 i hat minus 0.094 j hat meters. The conclusion. After 200 nanoseconds, the proton is located at approximately 0.15 i hat minus 0.094 j hat meters. The negative y component means the proton is below the x-axis at that instant. This is consistent with counterclockwise circular motion that is carried the proton through slightly less than one complete revolution. The problem. A particle moves in a circle of radius r equals 2.0 meters. During the time interval from t equals 1.5 seconds to t equals 4.0 seconds, its speed varies with time according to v of t equals c sub 1 minus c sub 2 over t squared. c sub 1 equals 4 meters per second c sub 2 equals 6 meters dot s. What is the total acceleration of the particle at t equals 2.0 seconds? Expand the drop down below to see the worked solution. The model. The particle undergoes non-uniform circular motion. Its acceleration has one component directed radially inward because the direction of velocity is changing and one component tan gentle to the circle because the speed is changing. These components are perpendicular so the total acceleration magnitude is found by combining them as perpendicular vector components. The math. Substituting t equals 2.0 seconds into the given speed function gives the instantaneous speed v of 2.0 equals 4.0 minus 6.0 over 2.0 squared equals 2.5 meters per second. The radio or centripetal acceleration is determined by the instantaneous speed and the radius of the circular path as a sub c equals v squared over r. Substituting the speed and radius gives the centripetal acceleration at the specified time a sub c equals 2.5 meters per second squared over 2.0 meters equals 3.1 meters per second squared. The tangential acceleration is the rate of change of the speed a sub t equals dv over dt. Since the speed function can be written as v of t equals 4.0 minus 6.0 t to the power of negative 2, differentiating the speed gives the tangential acceleration function a sub t equals 12.0 t to the power of negative 3. Substituting t equals 2.0 seconds gives the tangential acceleration a sub t equals 12.0 over 2.0 cubed equals 1.5 meters per second squared. Combining the perpendicular radio and tangential components gives the total acceleration magnitude magnitude of vector a equals square root of a sub c to the power of 2 plus a sub t to the power of 2 equals square root of 3.1 squared plus 1.5 squared meters per second squared equals 3.5 meters per second squared. Using the ratio of the inward component to the tangential component gives the direction measured inward from the tangent theta equals tan to the power of negative 1 of a sub c over a sub t equals tan to the power of negative 1 of 3.1 over 1.5 equals 64 degrees. The conclusion at t equals 2.0 seconds the particle has a centripetal acceleration of 3.1 meters per second squared inward and a tangential acceleration of 1.5 meters per second squared along the direction of motion. The total acceleration has magnitude 3.5 meters per second squared and points 64 degrees inward from the tangent.
